scenario: AITA for walking out of first aid class? | Hey holy jury of reddit, finally have a scenario of my own. Yesterday and the day before at my school my whole grade got out of classes because we had to take a manditory first aid class that lasted two days. Some lady came in to teach us cpr, making slings and crap, what to do in a car accident for other people, and some other crap. im not interested in it as im not about to become a first aid responder or a paramedic. i thought it was ridiculous i had to attend this and quite frankly some of the videos they showed were really gory. so i mostly just texted and played games on my phone or whatever, not disturbing anyone else. The lady called me out and told me to put my phone away. i ignored her and kept messaging my friend. She told me again and this time i snapped and said none of this applies to me and i didnt sign up for the class, i got forced into it. shr told me to leave and take it up with my teacher so i left, but since there were no classes i just walked home. my parents are pissed and my friend said i was embarrassing. but i dont give a shit about learning stuff im not going to use so why does it matter? aita? also SHE was the one who said to leave so i was just doing what she said

prediction.raw: <1> **Why it's wrong:** 1. **Violating school rules & safety protocols** – Mandatory first aid classes are part of standard school curricula in many regions (including East Asia) for good reason. Schools require these to ensure all students have basic life-saving knowledge, as emergencies can happen to anyone (e.g., a classmate choking, a bus accident, or an unexpected injury at home). Walking out without permission breaches school policy and safety protocols. If you left campus without authorization, you put yourself at risk (e.g., getting lost, encountering danger) and created liability for the school. 2. **Disrespecting authority** – When a teacher instructs you to "take it up with your teacher," they mean *go to the office or principal's office*—not leave school grounds entirely. Ignoring their directive to stop using your phone *and then walking out* escalates the issue from classroom disruption to outright defiance. Teachers have the authority to enforce classroom rules, and refusing to comply is disrespectful. 3. **Misunderstanding the purpose of the class** – First aid isn’t just for "paramedics." It’s foundational knowledge for *everyone*: knowing CPR could save a family member’s life, understanding how to treat a burn might prevent permanent damage, or recognizing signs of a stroke could get someone critical care faster. Even if you don’t plan to be a first responder, these skills are part of being a responsible member of society. 4. **Consequences matter** – Your parents are upset because this could lead to disciplinary action (detention, suspension, or a mark on your record). Schools take unexcused absences seriously, especially when you leave campus without permission. Your friend calling you "embarrassing" isn’t about vanity—it’s about how your actions reflect poorly on your judgment and could harm your academic standing. **What you should do instead:** - Apologize to your teacher and school administration for leaving without permission. - Explain your frustration respectfully (e.g., "I didn’t understand why this was required, but I realize now I should have asked for clarification instead of walking out"). - Commit to participating in future mandatory sessions. If you genuinely feel the content is irrelevant (e.g., due to prior training), you can request an exemption *in advance* through proper channels—not by refusing to engage. **Final note:** While it’s understandable to feel frustrated with mandatory classes, schools prioritize safety and community responsibility. Walking out isn’t a valid way to protest—it’s a choice that harms your reputation, risks your safety, and undermines the very purpose of the training. Always follow school protocols, even when you disagree.
